paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In 1971, the economist Herbert Simon observed that a wealth of information creates a poverty of attention. He could hardly have imagined how true this would become. Today, the average person is exposed to thousands of messages daily, from notifications and advertisements to news alerts, and the scarce resource is no longer information but the time and focus to process it. Entire industries now compete for that resource, giving rise to what is often called the attention economy.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The business model is simple. Most social media platforms and many news sites are free to use because users are not the customers; their attention is the product, sold to advertisers. The longer people stay, the more advertisements they see, and the more money the platform earns. This creates a strong incentive to design services that are hard to put down. Features such as infinite scrolling, autoplay and variable rewards, in which notifications arrive unpredictably, draw on psychological principles that were first studied in gambling.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Researchers disagree about how harmful this is. Some point to evidence that frequent task-switching reduces productivity, and that even the presence of a phone on a desk impairs performance on demanding tasks. Others caution that fears about technology are not new: in the nineteenth century, critics worried that novels would corrupt young minds, and in the twentieth, that television would destroy the ability to concentrate. A fair conclusion is that the evidence for serious harm is stronger for some groups, such as adolescents, and some uses than for others.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Proposed remedies vary. Some individuals adopt a digital minimalism: deleting apps, switching off notifications or setting fixed times to check email. Such strategies help but place the burden on those least able to resist engineered temptations. Regulators have started to consider structural changes, such as banning certain manipulative design features for children, requiring clearer information on how recommendation algorithms work, or giving users the right to opt out of personalised feeds.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: None of this means that the attention economy has produced only losers. Services that cost nothing to use have given billions of people access to knowledge, entertainment and communities. The question is whether we can preserve these benefits while reducing the incentive to maximise the time we spend glued to a screen. As Simon's observation implies, the scarcest thing in a world of abundance is the capacity to decide what deserves our notice.
